title: Harvesting heather honey
subtitle: Managing the late-season heather flow and pressing the thixotropic crop.
excerpt: Heather honey sets to a jelly in the comb within days of being laid down, and will not spin out in a normal extractor. It needs a honey press or a special loosener tool to break the gel before spinning, or the beekeeper harvests it as cut comb. Getting colonies to the moor at the right time, and getting them home before October colds, is as important as the pressing itself.
sourceNotes: BBKA Bee Craft, heather honey management articles (2018, 2020). Frank Pearson, Bee-keeping for All (1923), Internet Archive, chapter on heather honey. NBU Beekeeper's Toolkit (2024). Scottish Beekeepers Association, Heather Honey Guide (2022). R.O.B. Manley, Honey Farming (1946), chapter on moor management.

glossaryTerms.definition: A property of heather honey that makes it set to a gel when left undisturbed but return to a liquid when stirred or agitated. This prevents it being spun in a standard extractor without first breaking the gel.
Calluna vulgaris, the common heather of British moorland. Its late-summer flowers produce a dark, strongly flavoured honey with a distinctive gel character.
A fruit-press or purpose-built press that squeezes honey out of uncapped comb without spinning, used for honeys that cannot be centrifuged.
A metal needle board fitted to a power drill that punctures sealed heather comb to break the gel before the frames are spun in a standard extractor.

content.text: Heather honey is the last honey of the UK bee year, taken from
ling heather
on upland moors in August and early September. It is strongly flavoured, dark reddish-amber, and
thixotropic
: it sets to a gel in the comb and cannot be extracted by spinning without first breaking that gel. Harvesting it requires either a
honey press
or a
loosener tool
to puncture the sealed cells before spinning.
Moving colonies to the moor

Heather is a specialist crop that requires moving hives to the moor. The flow runs from early August to mid-September depending on altitude and season. Colonies should be on site by the end of July to allow bees to orientate before the main flow opens.
Take strong colonies only. A colony on eight or more brood frames with a good queen can work a heather flow productively. Weaker colonies will not build stores fast enough before September.
Fit the entrance reducer before moving. Move hives at night when all bees are in. Ventilate the hive during transport by fixing a mesh screen over the entrance rather than blocking it solid.
Set the hive on level ground, entrance facing away from prevailing wind and sheltered from early-morning sun if possible. Moors can be very exposed.
Check the colony a week after moving. Bees should have orientated and be foraging. Inspect for swarm cells: a colony that swarms on the moor is very difficult to retrieve.
Clearing the supers
Clear supers before the end of August if weather is deteriorating. Bees removed from the moor in September can be caught in cold snaps with insufficient winter stores.

Fit a clearer board below the supers in the early evening. Give it 2 to 3 days: heather honey is sticky and bees are reluctant to move down through a porter escape. Check the supers are clear before lifting.
Remove supers into a sealed van or car straight away. Heather-moor bees are defensive and will follow honey a long way.

Check stores remaining in the brood box before leaving the moor. A colony that has been working a heather flow hard may have very little honey left for winter. Feed sugar syrup on site or immediately on returning home.
Pressing or spinning

Extract heather honey as soon as possible after removing the supers. The longer it sits in capped comb at room temperature the more firmly the gel sets, and eventually it will not even press out cleanly.
Press method
Uncap the frames as usual using an uncapping fork or heated knife.
Cut the comb from the frames. Crush it coarsely by hand or with a clean wooden block.

Load into a muslin-lined honey press or a fruit press. Press slowly: heather honey is dense and needs time to flow through the muslin. A gentle first press, followed by a harder second press, extracts most of the honey.
Pass through a coarse strainer into a settling tank. Allow 48 hours to settle. Air bubbles from pressing take longer to clear than in spun honey.
Loosener and spin method
Uncap the frames. Push the loosener tool (a needle board fitted to a slow-speed drill) through both faces of each capped cell cluster, covering the full frame face.
Spin at low speed immediately after loosening, before the gel re-sets. Extract into a tank and strain.

Pressed heather honey often contains more pollen and wax particles than spun honey. It sets to a spreadable jelly in the jar within weeks. Many buyers prefer this texture and the stronger flavour. Label it separately from summer honey: it is a distinct product.

attrs.cue: Bees will not clear the supers through the clearer board
attrs.cause: Heather honey is heavy and tacky; bees resist moving through the porter escape when it is laden
attrs.fix: Give 72 hours rather than 24. On a warm day, place the clearer board and leave overnight before checking. If still not clear, use a bee brush and carry frames out individually.

attrs.cue: Honey will not press through muslin
attrs.cause: Gel has set too firmly; comb has been left too long
attrs.fix: Warm the pressing room to around 25 degrees. Do not heat above 35 degrees or the aromatic compounds that distinguish heather honey degrade. Warmth softens the gel enough to press.

attrs.cue: Colony returned from moor has very little winter stores
attrs.cause: Bees worked the flow so hard that they consumed their own reserves
attrs.fix: Feed 2:1 sugar syrup immediately. A colony short of stores after the heather season is unlikely to build up enough to survive winter without supplemental feeding.
